title: Ethics and Terms of Audit Engagements
outcomes: Explain the fundamental ethical principles and the conceptual framework.
Identify threats to independence and suitable safeguards; apply professional skepticism.
Apply SA 210 to preconditions, engagement letters and changes in terms.
Explain the elements of quality control under SQC 1.

meta.exam_tip: For each fact pattern, name the principle or threat first, then the safeguard or action.

concepts.title: Ethics and the fundamental principles
body: Ethics is a state of mind guiding conduct; the profession's value depends on public trust. The ICAI Code of Ethics follows a principles-based (conceptual framework) approach rather than only fixed rules.

Fundamental principles: integrity (straightforward and honest); objectivity (no bias, conflict of interest or undue influence); professional competence and due care (current knowledge and diligent work); confidentiality (no disclosure or use of information without authority or legal duty); and professional behaviour (comply with laws, avoid discrediting the profession).

Under the conceptual framework, the professional identifies threats to these principles, evaluates them, and applies safeguards to eliminate them or reduce them to an acceptable level — or declines or ends the engagement.
concepts.analogy: The Code supplies principles; the professional must apply judgement to each situation.
concepts.work: Using a client's confidential merger news to buy shares breaches confidentiality and integrity.

concepts.title: Independence: threats and safeguards; professional skepticism
body: Independence of mind (objective state of mind) and independence in appearance (avoiding facts that a reasonable person would see as compromising) are both required.

Threats: self-interest (financial interest, fee dependence, loans); self-review (auditing one's own work); advocacy (promoting the client's position); familiarity (long or close relationships); intimidation (pressure or threats).

Safeguards: those created by the profession, law or regulation (education, standards, monitoring, rotation requirements) and those in the work environment (firm policies, independent reviews, separate teams, rotation, communication with TCWG).

Professional skepticism is an attitude of questioning, alert to conditions that may indicate misstatement and to evidence that contradicts other evidence, and a critical assessment of evidence — neither assuming dishonesty nor unquestioned honesty.
concepts.analogy: Independence is what gives an audit opinion its value; skepticism is how it is exercised.
concepts.work: Accepting a CFO's explanation for unusual year-end sales without corroboration shows a lack of skepticism.

concepts.title: Agreeing the terms of audit engagements (SA 210)
body: SA 210: the auditor accepts an engagement only if preconditions exist — an acceptable financial reporting framework, and management's acknowledgement of responsibility for preparing the statements, for internal control, and for giving access to information and persons.

Terms are recorded in an engagement letter or other written agreement covering objective and scope, auditor's and management's responsibilities, the framework, and expected form of reports (with a note that content may differ). It may also cover planning, fees, use of experts and arrangements with predecessor auditors.
A limitation of scope imposed by management before acceptance, likely to result in a disclaimer, leads the auditor not to accept (unless required by law).

Change in terms: the auditor agrees only with reasonable justification; a request to change to a lower assurance engagement is not reasonable if it relates to incorrect, incomplete or unsatisfactory information. In recurring audits, the auditor considers whether terms need revising (e.g. change in management, ownership, legal requirements).
concepts.analogy: Clear terms prevent misunderstandings about what an audit is and is not.
concepts.work: A new law requiring additional reporting is a reason to revise the engagement letter.

concepts.title: Quality control (SQC 1)
body: Audit quality depends on the firm's system of quality control. SQC 1 requires firms to establish policies covering: leadership responsibilities for quality; relevant ethical requirements (including independence confirmations); acceptance and continuance of client relationships; human resources; engagement performance (direction, supervision, review, consultation, engagement quality control review); and monitoring.
Before accepting, the firm considers integrity of the client, competence and capabilities including time and resources, and compliance with ethical requirements.

Documentation of the system and monitoring of its effectiveness, including inspection of completed engagements, are required. (ICAI's newer Standard on Quality Management follows the same objectives with a risk-based approach.)
concepts.analogy: Quality is designed into the firm, not inspected into a single file at the end.
concepts.work: A firm that lacks staff with banking knowledge should decline a complex bank audit.

illustrations.title: Spot the threat
illustrations.q: Identify the threat to independence and a safeguard: (a) the audit partner's spouse holds shares in the client; (b) the firm prepared the client's accounts it now audits; (c) the firm defends the client's position before a tax tribunal; (d) the same partner has led the audit for many years and is close to the CFO; (e) the client threatens to change auditors unless a provision is dropped.

head: Case
Threat
Possible safeguard
rows: Dispose of the interest or remove the partner from the engagement
Separate teams with independent review, or decline the non-audit service where prohibited
Avoid such representation for audit clients where it compromises objectivity; use different personnel
Rotate the partner; engagement quality review
Discuss with those charged with governance; consult; withdraw if necessary
solution.title: Threats and safeguards

illustrations.title: Before saying yes
illustrations.q: A prospective client wants an audit but (a) refuses to acknowledge responsibility for internal control and (b) later, after acceptance, asks to change the engagement to a review because a bank loan is no longer needed. How should the auditor respond under SA 210?

head: Situation
Response
rows: Do not accept the engagement unless required by law; management must acknowledge responsibility for preparing the statements, for internal control and for giving access
(b) Request to change to a review

Consider whether the reason is reasonable: a genuine change in need may justify it; but a change to avoid an unfavourable finding or scope limitation does not. If unjustified and management will not let the audit continue, withdraw where possible and consider communication duties
solution.title: SA 210

jobs.title: Client acceptance file
jobs.situation: The firm is invited to audit a fast-growing listed company.
steps: Check integrity of owners and management.
Confirm independence of every team member.
Confirm preconditions and issue an engagement letter.
jobs.takeaway: Acceptance procedures protect the firm before any audit work starts.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a fundamental principle in the Code of Ethics?
mcqs.explain: The five principles cover honesty (integrity), freedom from bias (objectivity), skill with diligence (competence and due care), secrecy (confidentiality) and good conduct (professional behaviour). In practice: profitability is not an ethical principle.

mcqs.q: A threat arising when an auditor evaluates his own earlier work is:
mcqs.explain: Self-review threats arise when the auditor relies on judgements he made earlier. In practice: separate teams help.
mcqs.topic: Independence: threats and safeguards; professional skepticism

mcqs.q: Long association of a senior auditor with a client creates a:
mcqs.explain: Closeness reduces objectivity over time. In practice: rotation is a key safeguard.
mcqs.topic: Independence: threats and safeguards; professional skepticism

options: A questioning mind and critical assessment of evidence
mcqs.explain: Skepticism neither assumes dishonesty nor unquestioned honesty. In practice: corroborate unusual explanations.
mcqs.topic: Independence: threats and safeguards; professional skepticism

mcqs.q: A precondition for an audit under SA 210 is:
options: Management acknowledges responsibility for internal control
mcqs.explain: Management must accept responsibility for the statements, internal control and access. In practice: obtain it in writing.
mcqs.topic: Agreeing the terms of audit engagements (SA 210)

mcqs.q: A request to change an audit to a review because adverse findings are expected is:
options: A matter for the client only
mcqs.explain: Changes to avoid unfavourable outcomes are not reasonable. In practice: withdraw if necessary.
mcqs.topic: Agreeing the terms of audit engagements (SA 210)

mcqs.q: Engagement quality control review is part of which SQC 1 element?
mcqs.explain: Engagement performance covers direction, supervision, review, consultation and EQCR. In practice: required for listed entity audits.

mcqs.q: Holding shares in an audit client creates a:
mcqs.explain: Financial interest may bias judgement. In practice: dispose of the interest before accepting.
mcqs.topic: Independence: threats and safeguards; professional skepticism

summary: Five principles: integrity; objectivity; competence with due care; confidentiality; professional behaviour.
Threats: self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity, intimidation.
SA 210: preconditions, engagement letter, changes only with reasonable justification.
SQC 1: six elements of a quality control system.
remember: Independence of mind and in appearance are both needed.
traps: Change to a review to avoid adverse findings is not reasonable.

viva.model: Integrity and objectivity; professional competence with due care; confidentiality; and professional behaviour.
Avoiding facts and circumstances so significant that a reasonable and informed third party would conclude the auditor's objectivity has been compromised.
Rotation of senior personnel and an independent review by a partner not involved in the engagement, besides discussing with those charged with governance.

viva.q: What does an engagement letter contain?
viva.model: Objective and scope, responsibilities of auditor and management, the reporting framework, and the expected form of the auditor's reports.
Leadership, ethical requirements, acceptance and continuance, human resources, engagement performance and monitoring.

cases.title: CA Meera & Associates
cases.case: CA Meera & Associates audits Indus Foods Ltd. Facts: Meera's brother is the CFO of Indus; the firm also maintains Indus's books; fees from Indus are 40% of the firm's total fees; and the MD hints that the audit will be moved if the inventory provision is not reduced.

mcqs.q: The brother being CFO creates a:
mcqs.explain: A close family member in a key position at the client creates familiarity (and possibly self-interest) threats. In practice: such a relationship may make the threat unacceptable.
mcqs.topic: Independence: threats and safeguards; professional skepticism

mcqs.explain: Auditing records the firm itself prepared is self-review. In practice: such services are restricted for audit clients.
mcqs.topic: Independence: threats and safeguards; professional skepticism

mcqs.explain: Heavy reliance on one client's fees may influence judgement. In practice: consider pre- or post-issuance review.
mcqs.topic: Independence: threats and safeguards; professional skepticism

mcqs.explain: Pressure to change a judgement under threat of losing the audit is intimidation. In practice: escalate to the audit committee.
mcqs.topic: Independence: threats and safeguards; professional skepticism
